Rust is less of a game and more of a psychological experiment to see how long it takes for your faith in humanity to evaporate. You start with nothing but a rock and a torch, and somehow, by the end of your first hour, you're running naked through the woods, being chased by a man wearing a wolf's head and screaming profanities about your mother.

The gameplay is simple: gather resources, build a base, and try not to die. The reality? You’ll spend hours painstakingly constructing your dream fortress, only to log in the next day and find it reduced to rubble because someone named "xX420Sniper69Xx" decided your stash of raw chicken was worth a rocket launcher.

The graphics are stunning—just don’t stop to admire the scenery because that’s when Chad with an AK will pop out of the bushes and turn you into loot. And the community? Let’s just say it’s a beautiful mix of sociopaths, philosophers, and people who think "friendly" means "let me lull you into a false sense of security before stabbing you in the back."

But honestly, that's the charm of Rust. It's not about survival; it's about the stories. Like the time I joined a clan, only to be betrayed because I accidentally ate all the corn. Or the time I spent an hour taming a horse, only for it to immediately drown because I didn’t know horses can’t swim.

In conclusion, Rust is a masterpiece of chaos. It's frustrating, hilarious, and downright cruel—but you'll keep coming back because no other game lets you experience the raw thrill of chasing a fully geared player with nothing but a spear and blind optimism.

Rust is not about survival, it's about people. People think that Rust is about survival, about campfires, food, tools, and stone. No. Rust is about people, and people are worse than beasts. You meet a person, and he shouts to you: "friendly, friendly," throws you food, smiles, and ten minutes later you wake up without a sleeping bag, without loot, and without a home. And the scariest thing, you know what? That you are not even angry anymore, you expected it. In this game, you can't trust anyone, but for some reason, you still sometimes do. Rust is about betrayal, revenge, paranoia. It's not just a survival game, it's a real social experiment. And at some point, you become the one you used to hate. You raid newcomers, take the last cloth from homeless people, and set traps in the bushes. You just hated door campers, and five minutes later you are sitting with a shotgun at someone's house. Rust first breaks you, and then rebuilds you, but as a different person. In Minecraft, you build, in Alchemy, you follow, in The Forest, you defend, and in Rust, you learn to be a beast. And not because you want to, but because otherwise you simply won't survive. Yes, Rust gives you a sense of trust, but only to break it. There are no neutrals here, only enemies and not-yet-enemies. At first, you defend yourself, and then you learn to take revenge. Rust re-educates you, your morals adapt to a new world where kindness is a weakness. And gradually, you turn into the person you complained about in the first hours of the game.

50 hours in Rust and I have become a deeply unserious version of myself.

I downloaded this game thinking I was going to be some hardened survivor. A wasteland menace. A feared scavenger. A post-apocalyptic warlord.

In reality, I am a mostly naked man panic-jogging through the woods with 37 stone, a torch, and the survival instincts of wet bread.

I have lost fights I should not even be legally allowed to talk about. I have been beaten unconscious by people with less clothing and less to lose than me. I have screamed internally while trying to close a door that I built myself. I have crouched in bushes so long I started feeling like prey in a nature documentary.

At this point, half my Rust experience is just me hearing a footstep and instantly turning into a Victorian orphan.

I don't roam. I scurry.
I don't farm. I forage nervously.
I don't get into gunfights. I donate loot at high speed.

Every time I leave my base, I act like I'm going on a military operation, when really I'm just going out to hit a rock and maybe embarrass myself in a new location. I’ll spend 20 minutes gathering scrap, components, and enough hope to briefly believe in myself, only to get folded by some shirtless goblin with a crossbow who moves like he pays rent in the walls.

And the worst part is how pathetic I become the second I have good loot.

The moment I pick up anything valuable, I stop being a human being. I start moving like a rat that owes money. Every bush becomes a safe house. Every sound becomes a threat. Every shadow is a fully geared man named something like xX_CumProphet_Xx who has already decided my inventory belongs to him.

I have hidden in places no grown adult should ever have to hide. Behind barrels. Under stairs. In random corners of monuments, holding still like the game will forget I exist. I have watched other players run past me while I sat there clutching my stolen fuse and four scraps of dignity.

My combat strategy is mostly:

miss,

panic,

reload at the wrong time,

die in a way that teaches nothing.


I’ve lost bows to nakeds.
I’ve lost guns to people with spears.
I’ve lost full inventories because I got scared by a pig and ran directly into a road like a confused pensioner.

And don’t even get me started on base building. I built my first base like a proud little homeowner, stepped back to admire it, and somehow managed to lock myself out of it with all my materials inside. I have placed doors backwards, walls wrong, sleeping bags in stupid places, and boxes so badly that I trapped myself in my own airlock like an idiot in a homemade coffin.

At one point I was so desperate to avoid another player that I swam around an entire section of the map instead of just crossing the road. I drowned anyway.

Night time turns me into an actual coward. I hear one distant movement and suddenly I’m inside my base, lights off, not breathing, staring at my door like someone in a horror movie who knows they made bad choices. If someone jumps on my roof, my soul leaves my body and waits outside until morning.

I have been door camped so many times that opening my front door now feels like checking if the monster is still under the bed.

The animals are no better. Every boar, wolf, and bear in this game seems personally insulted by my existence. I don’t even react with fear anymore. I react with disappointment. Just this exhausted, silent acceptance that yes, of course the forest has sent another four-legged missile to ruin my afternoon.

And yet, every now and then, I do something incredible. I win a fight I had no business winning. I make it home stacked with loot. I close the door with 3 health left and just sit there in silence, staring at my screen like I survived a car crash.

Those moments keep me going. Those horrible, beautiful moments where I almost look competent.

Then I step on a bear trap, get shot in the head, and wake up on a beach again holding a rock like none of this ever mattered.

Rust is a survival game where the main thing you’re surviving is other players and your own terrible decisions. It is stressful, hilarious, mildly disturbing, and somehow still impossible to stop playing.

Recommended.

Rust is not a survival game. It is a psychological experiment disguised as a video game.

You spawn on a beach with absolutely nothing. No weapons. No clothes. No idea what you're doing. Five minutes later, some naked guy named xX_DeathDaddy_Xx has hit you in the head with a rock, stolen your hemp, and somehow built a mansion next to your corpse.

The game begins peacefully. You collect wood. You mine some stone. You build a tiny wooden house and think, “Finally, I'm safe.”

You are not safe.

You hear footsteps.

BOOM.

Your entire house has disappeared.

Rust turns ordinary human emotions into gameplay mechanics. Happiness is finding a gun. Fear is hearing footsteps outside your base. Anger is getting door-camped for 45 minutes. And pure hatred is finally getting enough loot to feel powerful, only to disconnect for ten minutes and come back to find your entire base has been turned into a parking lot.

And somehow, you keep playing.

The most insane part is that Rust creates stories without even trying. One minute you're peacefully farming trees. The next, you're forming a military alliance with three strangers from Germany because a naked man with a compound bow has declared war on your entire clan.

The community is also completely unhinged. Nobody trusts anyone. Someone can walk up to you saying, “Friendly?” and you already know there's a 90% chance you're about to experience a life-changing betrayal.

The graphics can look beautiful, the combat can be insanely satisfying, and the base-building is addictive. But the real reason Rust is so good is the tension. Every resource matters. Every gunshot makes you nervous. Every trip away from your base feels like you're carrying your entire bank account through a war zone.

Rust isn't fun because it's fair.

Rust is fun because it's absolutely fucking insane.

You don't play Rust to relax.

You play Rust to lose 14 hours of your life, scream at your monitor, question your friendships, destroy your sleep schedule, and then wake up the next day thinking:

“Alright. One more wipe.”

Rust isn't a game you "play" for an hour after work. It's a second job. If you actually want to compete, expect to put in 1,000+ hours just to understand the basics, and several thousand before you're consistently winning fights against experienced players. Every mistake is punished, and every lesson is learned the hard way.

The gunplay, building, monument runs, and raids create some of the most intense moments you'll find in any survival game. Winning a fight when you're outnumbered or successfully defending your base after hours of farming is incredibly satisfying because nothing is handed to you.

That said, Rust has a serious cheating problem. Depending on the server, you'll eventually run into players using ESP, aim cheats, or other hacks. It can completely ruin the experience when you lose hours of progress to someone who clearly isn't playing fairly. Facepunch and server admins do ban cheaters, but it often feels like they're always one step behind.

The skill ceiling is ridiculously high. Good players don't just have good aim they know recoil control, positioning, movement, game sense, resource management, base design, monument routes, and how to outplay entire groups. It's one of the few games where experience genuinely matters.

I bought Rust thinking it would just be another survival game I’d mess around in for a weekend. I’d seen clips of raids, roof camping, and funny naked players running around with rocks, and I figured: “Yeah, I’ll try it out. Looks chaotic but fun.”

That was one of the worst decisions I’ve ever made.

At first, Rust felt amazing. The tension of hearing footsteps outside your base, the fear when a helicopter flies overhead, the rush of finding your first gun — it was all addictive in a way I didn’t fully understand yet. I told myself I’d just play a couple hours… then suddenly it was 3 AM. Then 5 AM. Then the sun was coming up and I hadn’t slept.

Fast forward to 70+ hours, and I realized something terrifying: Rust didn’t just become a game I played — it became my entire life.

I stopped caring about other games. I stopped caring about my normal routine. I’d sit at my PC thinking about Rust even when I wasn’t playing. “Should I move my base?” “Did my doors decay?” “What if someone is raiding me right now?” I’d be lying in bed stressing about pixels in a video game like it was real life.

The thing about Rust is that it messes with your brain. You don’t just play it — you live in it. Every scrap matters. Every minute matters. Every decision feels high stakes. If you log off for too long, you might wake up to your base completely wiped and everything gone. That fear alone keeps you glued to your screen longer than any game ever should.

Socially, Rust also destroyed me for a bit. I stopped talking to friends as much. I skipped calls. I ignored messages because I was “busy defending base.” I’d tell people, “Yeah, I’ll hop off soon,” and then not log off for another four hours. My sleep schedule got absolutely cooked. I started staying up way too late, grinding for loot that would probably just get raided anyway.

And that’s the cruel joke of Rust — no matter how hard you work, you can lose everything overnight. You can spend 10 hours building a base, farming, crafting guns, grinding components… and then some sweaty clan comes along at 3 AM and blows it all up while you’re offline. All that effort? Gone. For nothing.

But here’s the worst part: even after all that, I still wanted to keep playing. Rust is rage-inducing, stressful, and sometimes downright miserable… yet it’s also insanely compelling. The highs are ridiculously high. Winning a big raid, surviving a crazy fight, or outsmarting other players feels better than almost any other game I’ve played.

So did Rust ruin my life? In a way… yeah. At least for a while. It turned me into a sleep-deprived grinder who cared way too much about a virtual base. It made me angry, paranoid, and obsessed. I lost track of time constantly.

But was it also one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve ever had? Also yes.

Rust isn’t just a game — it’s a psychological experiment disguised as a survival sandbox. If you value your time, your sleep, or your sanity… do not buy this game. But if you’re curious, reckless, and want to experience pure chaos, betrayal, adrenaline, and stress in digital form… welcome to Rust. You’ve been warned.

[h1] Before you scroll down and read the rest.. let me say one thing: "Rust is a high risk, high reward -type of game, if you get salty every time you die.. then move along.. this game isn't for you". [/h1]

[h1][b]General game information [/b][/h1]

This game is a great example of a survival sandbox game. You can literaly do whatever the hell you wanna do. Do you wanna roleplay? Go for it. Do you wanna build stuff and let your creative mind blow of some steam? Go for it. Do you wanna murder another player in cold blood with your trusted rock? Go for it.

Obviously there are populair ways (PVP) to play the game but when you spawn in this game.. naked and along on a beach.. armed with a rock and torch.. with nothing holding you back.. you will realise why you woke up on the beach in the first place.
_______________________________

[h1][b]My experience [/b][/h1]

At the time of writing this review i've been playing this game for years. It started out with a mate of mine buying the game. I was watching him through some streaming software and I thought it looked fun. So I bought it.
After figuring out the basics of crafting and resource gathering the two of us started building a wonderful base. That base lasted for a full hour. Then we were severly punished for the flaws in our design by a more experienced player. This happened over and over and over and over again. At this point a lot of people lose interest in the game, I didn't.
For some reason I was determined to learn from my previously made mistakes and improve on them.
This resulted in over 1800 hours of gameplay. 1800 of GLORIOUS hours. But like I said earlier, this game isn't for the feint of heart.
_______________________________

[h1][b]State of the Game [/b][/h1]

When you invest a little into this game physically and emotionally.. you will run into people referring to "Legacy" being the best state of the game, I disagree.
The current version of Rust is a combination of two previously tested systems of the game.
These are named: [b]The Blueprint system + The component system[/b].
Most Rust players will tell you that the blueprint system was the best system this game has ever seen. Over the last few years them tried different systems which generally didn't get any love.
A week ago (at the time of me posting this review) They revamped the system to the one I mentioned earlier.
[b]The Blueprint system + The component system[/b] - Aka the best system Rust has ever seen + new features of older failed systems revamped.
_______________________________

[h1][b]The pros [/b][/h1]
[list]
[*]If you use a microphone, you will have the most fun and random interactions you have ever experienced.
[*]There's a lot of ways to express your creativity. Basebuilding, gearsets, drawing penisses on other peoples bases.
[*]There is no real endgame, so you can set your own goals. Trust me when I say that those can be very rewarding.
[*]Its a great game for Youtube content (has profanity filter, auto censoring nudes ect.)
[*]Its a great game for Twitch content (has a streamer mode to hide from streamsnipers, has profanity filter, auto censoring nudes ect.)
[*]As a big community that really loves the game, but for the most part is filled with toxic players. (Like any other game these days)
[*]The game is constantly being developed. Weekly changes+additions with every patch.
[*]The game also has a great Dev team, they are hardworking and very dedicated
[/list]

[h1][b]The cons [/b][/h1]
[list]
[*]It has a big learning curve. The first thing you need to do is join a empty server and start figuring stuff out cause on a populated server you will get punished for it.
[*]A lot of people KoS in the current state of the game, which is fine for me cause im used to it. But if you are new it can be very offputting.
[*]The game has a very annoying memoryleak that will cause problems no matter how much GB you got in that godlike computer of yours. (they are working on it)
[*]Deciding on the correct server for you to join will directly affect how much fun the game is for you as a soloplayer.
[*]The official servers are terrible. There is hardly ever a admin in there to counteract a possible cheater. My advice: Stick to the community servers.
[*]The game uses a day/night cycle. During the night it truly is pitchblack and you wont be able to see a thing. Unless you have Nvidia, then you can just fire up the gamma and you'll be fine. Especially vs people that have a AMD graphics card. Its a annoying problem in the game thats currently being looked into.
[/list]
_______________________________

[h1][b]The future isn't set in stone. [/b][/h1]

Well, sorta. If you take a look at the facepunch website you will be able to see a roadmap. On this roadmap you will be able to find features and fixes they lined up for the game. Some will be added shortly and some will probably never see the light of day. Keep in mind the game is currently still early access and might change drasticly in a year. I've seen the game go through 3-4 different systems now. And all of them had fun aspects and negative ones.
_______________________________

[h1][b]Conclusion [/b][/h1]

If you are still interested after reading all this, definately buy the game. Over the years of me playing Rust, I've had the most interesting interactions and the most fun experiences ive ever had in a game.

Rust is one of those games that will either give you some of the best moments you’ve had in gaming or completely destroy your sanity. You spawn on a beach with a rock and a torch thinking you’re about to start a cool survival adventure. Five minutes later someone with 4,000 hours runs past you, calls you a slur, and hits you in the head with a spear. Welcome to Rust.

The game is basically about surviving, building a base, gathering resources, and trying not to lose everything you own every five minutes. At first you’re just hitting trees and rocks trying to make basic tools while praying nobody sees you. Eventually you build a small base and start feeling safe… which is exactly when someone with a rocket launcher shows up and deletes it from existence while you’re offline.

But somehow that’s also what makes Rust fun. Every bit of progress actually feels meaningful because you know you could lose it at any moment. When you finally manage to defend a raid, win a fight, or successfully raid someone else, it feels amazing. The player interactions are also completely unpredictable. One moment someone is helping you and giving you gear, the next moment someone else is chasing you across the map with a shotgun while yelling into the microphone.

The game can also be incredibly chaotic and hilarious. You’ll see things like naked players running around with spears, giant clans controlling entire areas, people blasting music through voice chat, and random alliances forming and breaking constantly. No two days on a Rust server ever feel the same.

That said, the game is definitely not for everyone. It can be extremely toxic, brutally unforgiving, and very time-consuming. If you don’t like losing your progress or dealing with other players trying to ruin your day, you might hate it. But if you enjoy intense survival games where anything can happen, Rust can easily become one of the most addictive games you play.

Overall, Rust is chaotic, stressful, sometimes unfair, but also one of the most unique multiplayer experiences out there. You will get betrayed, raided, and probably scream at your screen at least once… but you’ll still log back in the next day.

After nearly 3,500 hours I finally decided to review one of my favorite games on PC. In fact, it was the reason why I bought a gaming PC in the first place.

Pros:
- RAIDING - Raiding other groups, clans, or enemies provided me with many hours of tactical, engaging, and intense fights. It is one of the core aspects of the game, and is what kept me hooked for so long.

- PVP -Rust is one of those rare games that gets your heart rate pumping after killing a couple of enemies, and trying to loot all of their bodies while zig zagging your way to safely deposit your loot back home. All while your hands are shaking.

- BUILDING - The way that people build bases is constantly being changed through certain forced updates. You used to be able to build huge castles and compounds, but now the game has switched to a more bunker base style build. This change in style every once in a while is refreshing in the form of you aren't seeing the same base build over and over again from YouTube tutorials.

- ROLEPLAY - Facepunch has implemented many items that encourage friendly player to player interaction. From shop fronts and vending machines, to mailboxes and notes, and to the new furniture being added to the game, there is certainly a place for your casual gamer. 

Cons:
Don't get this game if you won't treat it like a full time job. You will be disappointed every time you login to find that your base has been raided by a bunch of high schoolers who can spend almost 12 hours a day on the game.

Unfortunately, many Rust players are way too serious about their loot. Meaning, they would rather offline raid a base in 30 minutes, than be challenged in an online raid that provides multiple hours of fun for both sides. Also, a lot of shit talking and bragging about loot in the public chat.

Hackers, scripters, and ban evaders are everywhere.

FPS Stutters. The game on the highest setting looks beautiful, but expect to take a huge performance hit once you are in a gunfight. I run on potato settings with a high end PC to make sure I don't dip to 10 fps if I get in a big gunfight.

Overall, the gameplay in Rust is extremely addicting and you forget what time it is in real life while playing. However, the fact that you have to treat this game like a full-time job and the terrible performance hits is what will kill the game. Still, it remains my favorite.
